extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, patent attorneys, and advanced law students
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on when combinations or improvements are patentable, how equivalents and aggregations are treated, rules on joint inventorship and assignment, and standards for who is the actual inventor. Focused on legal standards and illustrative case law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentable improvement — new and useful combination
rubrics_metrics.description: Improvements for which a patent may be granted must be new and useful within the meaning of the patent law; the requirement is satisfied if the combination is new and the machine is capable of being beneficially used for the purpose for which it was designed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The law does not require the improvement to be of such general utility as to supersede all other inventions accomplishing the same object. A change in an old machine that adapts it to a new and valuable use and actually produces a new and useful result may be patentable, whether the change is a new combination of parts or a material alteration of one or more devices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere aggregation vs patentable combination
rubrics_metrics.description: A mere aggregation of parts, where the patentee has not the exclusive right to either and in which the parts have no new operation and produce no result due to the combination itself, is not invention and is not patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The combination must be new and produce a new and useful result that is due to the co-operative or reciprocal action of the combined devices, not merely to the separate action of any one device. If each part performs independently and the superiority is simply the selection of better known parts, there is no invention. Examples and distinctions may require close discrimination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional equivalence in combinations (equivalents)
rubrics_metrics.description: A device which, both mechanically and practically, performs the same precise office of another device, in substantially the same manner, is the equivalent of the latter for purposes of a combination claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if the alleged equivalent also performs additional functions or has different mechanical features, if for the purposes and in the operation embraced by the claim it performs identically in the same way, it may be deemed an equivalent and its substitution can constitute appropriation/infringement. Improvements that add functions do not necessarily avoid being equivalents.

rubrics_metrics.name: New combination of old elements may be patentable
rubrics_metrics.description: A new combination of old and well-known things may be a proper subject for a patent if the mode of combination was new and produced a beneficial result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The specification must claim the new combination, not the old processes individually. Prior knowledge of the separate principles does not preclude patentability where the mode of combination is novel and yields a beneficial effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Description not claimed may be dedicated to the public
rubrics_metrics.description: If a previous patent describes something but does not claim it as new, there is a strong (perhaps conclusive) presumption that what is described and not claimed is given up to the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This presumption can in some cases be removed only by surrender and reissue under the statute providing for such correction. A subsequent patent cannot cover what was already validly claimed in a prior patent, but where the first patent's claim was invalidly overbroad and did not validly embrace the subject, a later patent on a distinguishable improvement may be allowed (e.g., O'Reilly v. Morse).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of prior patents on joint invention claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior separate patents held by inventors are strong evidence against a claim of joint invention but are not necessarily conclusive an absolute bar to a joint patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The facts and statutory context matter: courts have allowed joint patents following inconsistent prior separate patents where the circumstances (e.g., innocence, mistake, or subsequent joint application) support it. Remedies for conflicting outstanding patents may include equity proceedings to declare patents void or other statutory remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory contemplation of joint invention and joint patents
rubrics_metrics.description: The statute contemplates the case of a joint invention and a joint patent; joint inventors may apply for and obtain a joint patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although some statutory language (in later acts) uses the singular for 'inventor' in parts of the specification/oath provisions, the obvious intent is to permit specification and oath to be signed by joint inventors when applying by joint petition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution on application by one for a joint patent or after assignment
rubrics_metrics.description: Where one party only applies for a patent acting for both joint inventors, or where one joint inventor assigns his interest before application, questions arise as to whether a patent for a joint invention can be issued to the joint inventors on the application of one, or whether it should be applied for as a several invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is prudent to avoid raising such questions if practicable. The effect of assignments before application may rest on common-law principles and the peculiar facts; statutory changes (e.g., making inventions assignable before application) affect the analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentee presumed to be the inventor; burden of proof
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a presumption of law that the patentee was the inventor of that which he patented; whoever alleges the contrary bears the burden of proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determination of inventorship is a mixed question of law and fact; general principles help guide the investigation into the process of forming or realizing the invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test for when suggestions from others invalidate a patent
rubrics_metrics.description: To invalidate a patent on the ground that the patentee received the suggestion of the invention from another, it is not enough to show the bare idea was suggested; the question is whether the principle or plan of the invention was substantially communicated so that nothing remained for the patentee to do except apply the skill of a constructor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If suggestions supplied all information necessary to construct a complete and perfect machine (i.e., they went to make up a complete machine), the patent is invalid because the real discovery belongs to another. If something remained for the patentee to devise or work out by his own skill, the patentee is the true inventor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of practical assistance/skill vs conception of plan
rubrics_metrics.description: Two general classes: (a) where the plan/conception came from another and the patentee only supplied mechanical details; (b) where the patentee conceived the plan but derived practical knowledge or manual skill from others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In class (a) the patent may be invalid if the plan was substantially communicated; in class (b) the patentee may still be inventor if others only provided practical skills or helped realize the conceived plan. The legal test focuses on whether the essential conception belonged to the patentee.

rubrics_metrics.name: Master-workman/employee-suggestion rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a master-workman conceived the plan and was engaged in experiments to perfect it, suggestions from an employed person during such experiments are not sufficient to deprive the employer of exclusive property in the perfected improvement unless such suggestions amount to a new method or arrangement that is itself a complete invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by Agawam Co. v. Jordan: suggestions that are merely auxiliary parts of the employer's invention, and that do not form any separate complete combination, do not defeat the employer's patent rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substitution that produces reciprocal action distinguishes patentable combination
rubrics_metrics.description: A combination is patentable where there is a reciprocal action or operation of the parts upon each other and conjointly upon the entire machine, each part giving increased support and efficiency to the other, producing a new efficiency due to the combination itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast with mere aggregation where parts operate independently. The example of flanged collars combined with tenoned spokes: combined they provide mutual support and a stronger wheel; that reciprocal interaction supports a combination claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surrender and reissue as remedy for undesired dedication
rubrics_metrics.description: Surrender and reissue under the statute that provides for correction of inadvertency may remove the presumption that parts of a specification not claimed are dedicated to the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an inventor described but did not claim subject matter in a first patent and wishes to reclaim it, surrender and reissue may be the available statutory route, subject to the limitations of the reissue provisions and the status of prior claims.
